about: Knowledge base behind the interactive solar system at /constellations. Moon counts are as of 2025 and keep changing as new moons are found.

sources.orbits: JPL approximate Keplerian elements (Standish), valid 1800 to 2050
sources.stars: d3-celestial star and constellation data, BSD-3-Clause

bodies.name: Sun
bodies.tag: The star that holds it all together
bodies.about: A middle-aged yellow dwarf about 4.6 billion years old. It fuses hydrogen into helium in its core, and that energy powers almost everything that happens on Earth. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a red giant.
stats: 25 days at the equator, about 35 at the poles
facts: It holds about 99.86% of all the mass in the solar system.
Sunlight reaches you in about 8 minutes 20 seconds, but the energy spent many thousands of years working its way out from the core first.
It loses about 4 million tonnes of mass every second, turned directly into energy.
Its outer atmosphere, the corona, is over a million degrees, far hotter than the surface below it. Why is still an active research question.
It does not rotate as a solid ball: the equator spins faster than the poles.
It circles the Milky Way about once every 230 million years, so it has made only about 20 laps in its life.

bodies.name: Mercury
bodies.about: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere to hold heat, so it has the widest temperature swing of any planet, and its huge iron core makes up most of its radius.
facts: One sunrise-to-sunrise day lasts two of its years.
Despite being closest to the Sun, it has water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters.
It is shrinking. As its core cools, the whole planet contracts and its crust wrinkles into cliffs hundreds of kilometres long.
It is not the hottest planet. Venus is, even though it is almost twice as far from the Sun.
A tiny mismatch in its orbit could not be explained by Newton, and explaining it was an early triumph for Einstein's general relativity.

bodies.name: Venus
bodies.about: Nearly Earth's size, wrapped in thick carbon dioxide and clouds of sulfuric acid. A runaway greenhouse effect keeps the surface hot enough to melt lead, day and night, pole to pole.
facts: It spins once in 243 Earth days but orbits in 225, so its rotation takes longer than its year.
It spins backwards compared with most planets, so the Sun would rise in the west.
Surface pressure equals being about 900 metres underwater on Earth.
The longest any lander has survived on the surface is about two hours: the Soviet Venera 13 in 1982.
Its clouds race around the planet in about four Earth days, far faster than the planet itself turns.

bodies.name: Earth
bodies.tag: The only place known to have life
bodies.about: The largest rocky planet and the only world known to have stable liquid water on its surface and life. Its magnetic field and atmosphere shield the surface from much of the Sun's radiation.
facts: The seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
A true rotation takes 23 hours 56 minutes. The 24-hour day includes the extra turn needed to face the Sun again.
Measured from Earth's centre, the farthest point is the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador, not Everest, because Earth bulges at the equator.
Days are slowly getting longer, because the Moon's tides act as a brake on Earth's spin.
You are moving at about 30 km per second around the Sun right now.

bodies.name: Moon
bodies.about: Most likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth. Its gravity drives most of Earth's tides and helps steady Earth's tilt.
facts: It drifts about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.
We always see the same side because it rotates exactly once per orbit. The far side is not permanently dark, though.
All the other planets could fit, just barely, in the average gap between Earth and the Moon.
With no wind or rain, the Apollo footprints could last for millions of years.
It is about 400 times smaller than the Sun and about 400 times closer, which is why total solar eclipses fit so neatly.

bodies.name: Mars
bodies.tag: The cold desert that once had rivers
bodies.about: A cold, dusty world with a thin atmosphere, and clear signs that liquid water once flowed across its surface. Its red colour comes from iron oxide, which is rust.
facts: Sunsets on Mars are blue, because fine dust scatters light differently from our air.
Olympus Mons is the tallest known volcano in the solar system, about 22 km high and about 600 km across.
Valles Marineris runs about 4,000 km, roughly the width of the United States.
Its moon Phobos is spiralling inward and should break apart or crash within about 50 million years.
Dust storms can grow to wrap the entire planet for weeks.
As far as we know, Mars is the only planet inhabited entirely by robots.

bodies.name: Jupiter
bodies.tag: The giant that shapes everyone's orbit
bodies.about: A gas giant more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. It has no solid surface, and its bands are jet streams in an atmosphere of hydrogen and helium.
facts: It has the shortest day of any planet, under 10 hours, and spins so fast that it visibly bulges at the equator.
The Great Red Spot is a storm observed for at least about 150 years, and it has been shrinking.
Its moon Ganymede is larger than the planet Mercury.
Its moon Io is the most volcanically active place in the solar system.
Jupiter and the Sun orbit a shared point that lies just outside the Sun's surface.
Jupiter has faint rings. They are made of dust and were only found in 1979.

bodies.name: Saturn
bodies.about: A gas giant famous for its vast ring system, made of countless pieces of water ice from dust size to house size. It is the least dense planet in the solar system.
facts: It is less dense than water, so it would float, given a big enough bathtub.
The main rings span about 280,000 km but are typically only about 10 metres thick.
A six-sided jet stream, a hexagon wider than Earth, circles its north pole.
Its moon Titan has rivers and lakes of liquid methane and an atmosphere thicker than Earth's.
Its moon Enceladus sprays water from a hidden ocean into space, which makes it a top target in the search for life.
The rings may be far younger than the planet, and they are slowly raining onto Saturn.

bodies.name: Uranus
bodies.tag: The planet that rolls on its side
bodies.about: An ice giant tipped so far over that it effectively orbits on its side. It was the first planet found with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781.
facts: Its axis is tilted about 98°, likely the result of an ancient giant collision.
Each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.
It has the coldest atmosphere of any planet, colder than Neptune even though it is closer to the Sun.
Its moons are named after characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope, not from mythology.
Only one spacecraft has ever visited: Voyager 2 flew past in 1986.

bodies.name: Neptune
bodies.tag: Found with math before anyone saw it
bodies.about: The most distant planet, a dark, cold ice giant with the fastest winds ever measured on a planet. Its existence was predicted from wobbles in the orbit of Uranus.
facts: It was located in 1846 almost exactly where mathematics said it should be.
It completed its first full orbit since discovery only in 2011.
Winds there reach about 2,000 km per hour, the fastest measured on any planet.
It gives off about 2.6 times as much heat as it receives from the Sun.
Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards, which suggests it was captured from the Kuiper Belt.
Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach it. From Neptune, the Sun looks like a very bright star.

bodies.name: Pluto
bodies.tag: Hasn't finished one orbit since we found it
bodies.about: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, reclassified in 2006. In 2015 New Horizons revealed mountains of water ice, nitrogen glaciers and a huge heart-shaped plain.
facts: It was discovered in 1930 and will not complete its first orbit since then until the 2170s.
It is smaller than Earth's Moon.
Its orbit is so stretched that it sometimes comes closer to the Sun than Neptune, yet the two can never collide.
Pluto and its moon Charon always show each other the same face, locked like dancers holding hands.
It was named by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old from Oxford.

bodies.name: Halley's Comet
bodies.tag: On its way back, due in 2061
bodies.about: The best-known periodic comet, visible to the naked eye about once in a human lifetime. Its orbit runs backwards compared with the planets and reaches beyond Neptune.
facts: Debris it leaves behind causes two meteor showers every year: the Eta Aquariids and the Orionids.
It appears on the Bayeux Tapestry, which records its 1066 return.
Mark Twain was born during its 1835 visit and died the day after it passed closest to the Sun in 1910.
Edmond Halley predicted its return, but died before he could see that he was right.
Its nucleus is one of the darkest objects known, darker than coal.

general.t: Everything you can see with your naked eye in the night sky is inside our galaxy, except a few galaxies such as Andromeda and the Magellanic Clouds.
If the Sun were a 10 cm ball, Earth would be a 1 mm grain 11 metres away, Neptune would be 320 metres away, and the next star would be about 2,900 km away.
The asteroid belt is nothing like the movies. On average its objects are so far apart that spacecraft cross it without having to dodge anything.
All the asteroids combined have less mass than our Moon.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object. Its signal takes almost a full day to reach Earth.
The Sun's gravity dominates out to the hypothesized Oort Cloud, perhaps a light-year or more away, far beyond every planet.
Constellations are mostly illusions of perspective. Stars in the same pattern can be hundreds of light-years apart from each other.
There are exactly 88 official constellations, and since 1930 they have been defined as regions that cover the entire sky, not just patterns.
The Big Dipper is not a constellation. It is an asterism, a pattern inside Ursa Major.
Polaris has not always been the North Star. Earth's axis wobbles over about 26,000 years, and Vega will take a turn around the year 13,700.
The Sun passes through 13 constellations each year, not 12. It spends more time in Ophiuchus than in Scorpius.
When you look at Deneb tonight, you are seeing light that left it roughly 2,600 years ago, though its distance is uncertain.
Stars do not actually twinkle. Earth's turbulent air makes them appear to. From orbit they shine steadily.
The planets all orbit in nearly the same flat plane because they formed from a single spinning disc of gas and dust.
Sunlight reaching Neptune takes about 4 hours, but light from the nearest other star takes over 4 years to reach us. The gap between stars dwarfs everything in this view.

And: It contains the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away, the most distant thing most people can see with the naked eye.
Aqr: It holds TRAPPIST-1, a small star with seven Earth-sized planets.
The Helix Nebula here is one of the closest planetary nebulae to Earth.
Aql: Its brightest star, Altair, spins so fast, about every 9 hours, that it is visibly flattened.
Boo: In 1933 light from its star Arcturus was used to switch on the lights of the Chicago World's Fair.
CMa: It holds Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, just 8.6 light-years away.
Sirius has a tiny white dwarf companion, about the size of Earth but with about the mass of the Sun.
Car: It holds Canopus, the second-brightest night star, which spacecraft have used as a navigation reference.
Eta Carinae is a monster star system that may explode as a supernova in the astronomically near future.
Cas: Its W shape is easy to find in the northern sky.
Tycho Brahe watched a supernova here in 1572, which helped overturn the idea that the heavens never change.
Cen: It contains Alpha Centauri, the nearest star system to the Sun at about 4.4 light-years.
Omega Centauri is the largest globular cluster in the Milky Way, with about 10 million stars.
Cru: It is the smallest of all 88 constellations.
It appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil and others.
Cyg: Cygnus X-1 here was the first object widely accepted as a black hole.
NASA's Kepler telescope stared at this patch of sky and found thousands of exoplanets.
Gem: Castor looks like one star but is actually a system of six.
The Geminid meteors come from an asteroid, 3200 Phaethon, not a comet.
Hya: It is the largest of all 88 constellations.
Leo: The Leonid meteor shower appears to radiate from here each November and has produced true meteor storms.
Lyr: Vega was the first star other than the Sun to be photographed, in 1850.
Vega was the North Star around 12,000 BC and will be again.
Oph: The Sun passes through it for about 18 days each year, yet it is not in the traditional zodiac.
Kepler's Supernova of 1604, the last one clearly seen in our galaxy with the naked eye, happened here.
Ori: Betelgeuse, its red shoulder, dimmed dramatically in 2019 and 2020 after ejecting a cloud of dust.
The Orion Nebula, about 1,340 light-years away, is an active stellar nursery you can see with binoculars.
Its stars look like a group but sit at very different distances from us.
Peg: 51 Pegasi b, found here in 1995, was the first planet discovered around a Sun-like star.
Per: Algol, the Demon Star, visibly dims every 2.9 days as a companion star passes in front of it.
The Perseids, one of the best yearly meteor showers, appear to come from here.
Sgr: The centre of the Milky Way, and its supermassive black hole, lie in this direction.
Its brightest stars form an asterism known as the Teapot.
Sco: Its red heart, Antares, means rival of Mars. If placed at the Sun, it would reach beyond the orbit of Mars.
Ser: It is the only constellation split in two pieces, separated by Ophiuchus.
Tau: The Pleiades star cluster is here. Many cultures tell stories of seven sisters about it.
The Crab Nebula is the remnant of a supernova that observers recorded in 1054.
UMa: The Big Dipper is only part of this much larger constellation.
Five of the Big Dipper's seven stars really do travel together through space.
Mizar and Alcor, in the handle, have been used as a naked-eye vision test.
UMi: It holds Polaris, which stays nearly still as the sky turns around it.
Polaris is not especially bright. It ranks only around 50th in the sky.
Vir: It is the largest zodiac constellation and the second largest overall.
The first image of a black hole, in the galaxy M87, was captured in this direction in 2019.
